setup.name: Required health signs and posters
setup.note: Seen at NYC Health: the choking first aid poster, CPR equipment notice, food allergy poster, no smoking sign and alcohol-pregnancy sign are free by calling 311. The $25 for frames and tape and the 5 days of mail are my estimate. Should be required in every kit: the lead or the assembler can flip the flag once kits include it.

setup.name: Allergy statement on menus and allergy poster for staff
setup.agency: NYS Department of Health / NYC DOHMH
setup.note: Public Health Law §1356: the notice must appear on each menu, on online ordering pages, and on a staff poster in the workers' languages. $60 to reprint a menu board and paper menus is my estimate; the poster is free. Should be required in every kit.

setup.name: Workplace posters, 'Your Rights at Work' notice, harassment policy
setup.agency: NYS Department of Labor; NYC DCWP
setup.note: All required posters and the state's model harassment policy and training are free downloads from the agencies (NYS DOL posting requirements page; DCWP). The cost is $0 by design; mailers that bill $92.58 for a 'mandatory poster' are a known scam (BBB Scam Tracker). Should be required in every kit.

setup.name: No smoking and no vaping signs, written smoking policy
setup.note: NYC Health: owners must post the signs and adopt a written smoking and e-cigarette policy shared with staff. Signs are free from the city; $0 is by design.

setup.name: City practice inspection before the first graded one
setup.note: NYC Health: a new restaurant may request one consultative inspection for $100 after it has begun serving food and before its first graded inspection ($400 for a restaurant already graded). No violations are written unless a public health hazard cannot be fixed on the spot. The 14 days of waiting are my estimate; the city publishes no service time.

setup.name: FDNY open flame permit (candles)
setup.note: FDNY Restaurant Fire Safety Guide: the open flame permit's yearly inspection fee is $210. The 30 days of waiting are my estimate; FDNY publishes no service time. Needed only if you put candles on tables.

setup.name: Sign permit and licensed sign hanger
setup.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: a sign over 6 square feet needs a permit, and the installation must be done by a licensed sign hanger. The $1,500 for the filing, the hanger and the insurance certificate and the 30 days are my estimate; quotes vary widely. Not needed for a sign of 6 square feet or less. This is on top of the pack's $1,500 line for making the sign.

setup.name: Backflow device test and first report
setup.note: The yearly test report is the legal duty (15 RCNY §20-04(e), seen in the OATH penalty schedule). $240 per test is my estimate from plumbers' advertised ranges of $150 to $350. If the space has no device at all, installing one is plumbing work with filed plans and costs thousands: check before signing the lease.

setup.name: Portable ramp, doorbell and a lowered counter section
setup.note: My estimate: an aluminum portable ramp for one step ($300-$700), a wireless doorbell with a sign ($50), and carpentry for a 36-inch-high section of counter ($800). A small business gets back 50% of access spending between $250 and $10,250 as the federal Disabled Access Credit, up to $5,000 a year (IRS Form 8826): about $675 of this.

setup.name: Website and online menu a screen reader can use
setup.note: My estimate for a small site: text alternatives for images, a real text menu instead of a photo or PDF, labeled buttons, and a check with a screen reader. Why it matters: 3,117 federal website accessibility suits in 2025, 1,021 of them in New York (Seyfarth Shaw).

setup.name: Trademark search and federal application for the shop's name
setup.note: The search is free. The $350 filing fee per class and the roughly one year to registration are from memory of the 2025 USPTO fee schedule; I did not open it this session. Why it matters: a renamed Michigan cafe paid about $5,000 after a chain sued, against an estimated $50,000 to fight.

monthlyCosts.name: Background music license
monthlyCosts.note: A business music service with the performance licenses included: vendors advertise roughly $17 to $50 a month in 2026; $35 is my midpoint. Buying the licenses directly costs $636 to $1,600 a year for a small cafe (ASCAP from $324-$502, BMI from about $312, SESAC from $580, per vendor guides). Follows the 'music' lever: the default option costs this much.

levers.name: Music

options.label: Licensed background music service for businesses
Your own playlists with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC licenses
No music
Your personal streaming account on the shop speakers

levers.note: Vendor guides for 2026: ASCAP from $324-$502 a year, BMI from about $312-$415, SESAC from $580: $636 to $1,600 a year for a small cafe, here $110 a month for all three. Business music services that include the licenses advertise roughly $17 to $50 a month; $35 is my midpoint. Quality effects are design values.

levers.name: Practice inspections

options.label: None: the first inspector you meet is the real one
One city consultative inspection a year
Private food safety consultant every quarter

levers.note: Seen at NYC Health: a consultative inspection costs $400 for a restaurant that has already been graded ($100 once for a new one before its first graded inspection); it produces no violations unless a public health hazard cannot be fixed on the spot. $400 / 12 = $33, rounded to $35. The private consultant at about $350 a visit, four visits a year, is my estimate. In the proposed inspection model (extra.mechanics.inspection_score_and_grade) a practice inspection removes the general violations a new owner does not know about.

levers.name: Handling pastries and garnishes

options.label: Tongs, tissue and gloves for anything ready to eat
Bare hands, faster line

levers.note: $40 a month of deli tissue and gloves is my estimate from restaurant-supply prices. The violation and its fine are in violations.bare_hand_contact.

levers.name: What goes in the takeout bag

options.label: Straws, forks and napkins only when the customer asks
Everything in every bag, no questions

levers.note: $25 a month of extra straws, forks and napkins is my estimate. The legal option is also the cheaper one; the illegal one only saves a few seconds per order.

levers.name: When someone says they are an inspector

options.label: Staff check the photo ID and badge, call you, and let the inspector work
Staff say the owner is out and keep them waiting
Staff do whatever anyone with a clipboard says, cash included

levers.note: A standing instruction, free either way. The first option also defeats impostors (extra.eventCatalog.fake_inspector_visit): real inspectors never take payment on the spot; fines are paid to the city after a hearing. The third option has no violation; it loses money to scams.

levers.name: When a worker complains about pay or safety

options.label: Hear it, check the records, fix what is wrong
Cut their shifts until they quit

levers.note: A standing instruction. Punishing a complaint turns one wage question into a second, bigger case (violations.retaliation_firing).

levers.name: Help-wanted ads

options.label: Pay range in every ad; no questions about convictions before an offer
"Barista wanted, DM us" with no pay range

levers.note: A standing instruction, free either way. The Fair Chance Act also bars any question about criminal history before a conditional job offer (NYC Commission on Human Rights).

levers.name: Floors and entrance

options.label: Entrance mats, wet-floor signs and a mopping log
Mop when someone notices

levers.note: $45 a month for a rented entrance mat service and signs is my estimate. No violation attaches to the second option; it feeds the slip-and-fall exposure in extra.mechanics.private_lawsuits. A dated mopping log is what an insurer's lawyer asks for first.

levers.name: Legal help

options.label: Handle summonses and letters yourself
Hospitality lawyer on call and a representative for city hearings

levers.note: $150 a month is my estimate of a small retainer; no public price list exists. In the proposed hearing model (extra.mechanics.oath_hearing_choices) representation means no missed hearings and the mitigated penalty wherever the schedule offers one. OATH's own Help Center is free.

levers.name: Labels on food you pack yourself

options.label: Printed label with ingredients and major allergens on every wrapped item
A sticker with the name, nothing else

levers.note: Public Health Law §1357, in force since November 12, 2026: food prepared, packed and sold on the same premises must carry a label that names its major allergens. $30 a month for a label printer's rolls is my estimate. The law itself sets no penalty; the game charges the allergy-notice violation, and the larger exposure is the allergic-reaction claim in extra.lawsuits.

shortcuts.name: Take down the B
shortcuts.what: A B or C card in the window scares off walk-ins. Leave the old A up, or 'lose' the new card, and keep about 3% of sales. The card has a serial number and inspectors and neighbors check: $500-$1,000 for no card, $1,000-$2,000 for removing or faking it.
shortcuts.note: The 3% is my estimate. Evidence of direction and size: a study of more than 15,000 NYC restaurants over 28 months found A grades raise revenue and lower the chance of closing, and C grades lower revenue compared with B (Silver, Rothbart and others, Public Administration Review, 2019); a Los Angeles sales-tax analysis put an A at up to +6% and a B at +1-2%, a gap of about 4 points.

shortcuts.name: Skip the yearly backflow test
shortcuts.what: The valve on your water line must be tested every year by a certified tester, about $240 a visit. Skip it and save $20 a month. The city knows from its own records which reports are missing: $500, or $50 if you file before the hearing.
shortcuts.note: The $240 price of a test is my estimate from plumbers' advertised ranges ($150-$350); no official price exists.

shortcuts.name: Let the extinguisher tags expire
shortcuts.what: Two extinguishers need a certified company once a year, about $120, and a signed check every month. Skipping saves $10 a month. A fire inspector reads the tag first: $600, or $300 if fixed before the hearing.
shortcuts.note: The $120 a year for two units is my estimate from service companies' advertised prices; no official price exists.

shortcuts.name: Stack deliveries in the back exit
shortcuts.what: No storage room, so milk crates and cup cases live in the rear corridor. Saves about $150 a month of off-site storage or lost seats. A blocked exit is $950, or $475 if cleared before the hearing, and the first thing a fire officer looks at.
shortcuts.note: The $150 is my estimate of a small self-storage unit in the outer boroughs.

shortcuts.name: Pack the room on event nights
shortcuts.what: Open mic, launch party, 90 people in a room approved for far fewer: about 2% more sales a month. Overcrowding is $950 the first time and $2,375 the second, and the fire officer can empty the room mid-event.
shortcuts.note: The 2% is my estimate: two packed evenings a month at double the usual evening sales.

shortcuts.name: Candles on the tables, no permit
shortcuts.what: Candles make the evening. The FDNY open flame permit costs $210 a year; skipping it saves $18 a month. Open flame without the permit: $700, or $350 if you get the permit before the hearing.

shortcuts.name: Renovate without a Buildings permit
shortcuts.what: A handyman moves the sink, adds outlets and a wall over a weekend: no architect, no filing, no waiting. One neighbor's 311 call brings a Stop Work Order and a penalty of 21 times the permit fee, $6,000 at the least, and you file the plans anyway.
shortcuts.note: A one-time decision during build-out: it saves the architect, expediter and filing fees (the pack's $7,000 line) and the weeks of waiting. Shown here as $600 a month for 12 months until the engine supports one-time shortcuts.

shortcuts.name: Keep building under a Stop Work Order
shortcuts.what: Every month the order hangs on the door is a month of rent with no sales, so the crew works at night. Saves a month of rent each month. Working through the order is $6,000 each time it is caught, and a crime.

shortcuts.name: Hang the big sign without a permit
shortcuts.what: A sign over 6 square feet needs a permit and a licensed sign hanger: about $1,500 and a month of waiting. A friend with a ladder does it Saturday. If someone reports the block's signs to 311, the fine starts at $6,000.
shortcuts.note: A one-time decision: the $1,500 for the filing and the licensed sign hanger is my estimate; shown as $125 a month for 12 months until the engine supports one-time shortcuts.

shortcuts.name: Stop sweeping the sidewalk
shortcuts.what: Nobody sweeps the sidewalk and the 18 inches of gutter in front of the shop: about 15 minutes a day, $85 a month. Sanitation agents ticket during two posted hours a day: $100 to $300 each, sidewalk and gutter separately.
shortcuts.note: 15 minutes a day x 30 days x $17.00 an hour = $127; I count two thirds of it because some sweeping happens anyway.

shortcuts.name: Trash bags on the curb, no bins
shortcuts.what: Bags go out at closing with no lidded bin, or the bins stay out all morning. Saves the bins and a few minutes a day, about $20 a month. $50 the first time, $100 the second, $200 every time after, and bags on the curb feed the rats that cost you points.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: two 44-gallon lidded bins at about $120 each, replaced every year.

shortcuts.name: No carter: use the corner baskets
shortcuts.what: Cancel the private carter and drop the shop's bags in public litter baskets or the building's residential pile: saves about $250 a month. Agents open the bags and find your receipts: $100 to $300 each time.

shortcuts.name: A-frame sign in the middle of the sidewalk
shortcuts.what: A chalkboard out by the curb catches people from both directions: about 1% more sales. A sign may not stand more than 3 feet from your wall; farther out it is an obstruction: $100, then up to $300.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate; no measurement of A-frame signs on sales was found.

shortcuts.name: Buy foam cups
shortcuts.what: Foam hot cups cost about a cent and a half less than paper and need no sleeve: about 0.2% of sales. Foam cups and containers have been banned in New York City since 2019: $150, then $250, then $500.
shortcuts.note: 1.5 cents saved per $8.50 order = 0.18% of sales; cup prices from the pack's supplies line.

shortcuts.name: Speaker at the open door
shortcuts.what: Music out onto the sidewalk pulls people in: about 1% more sales. The people upstairs call 311; a reading over 42 decibels inside their apartment costs $2,000, then $4,000, then $6,000.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate.

shortcuts.name: Add a card fee at the register
shortcuts.what: A 3.5% fee appears on the card reader, not on the menu: it wipes out your card costs, about 3% of sales. The law allows a credit card surcharge only if the full card price is posted and it is no more than your real cost: up to $500 per violation.
shortcuts.note: 3.5% on the 90% of sales paid by card (the pack's card model) = 3.15% of sales.

shortcuts.name: Dogs welcome inside
shortcuts.what: Dog owners become regulars: about 1% more sales. A pet inside a food shop is a critical violation: $200 to $350 and 5 or more points toward your grade. Only service animals may come in; pets may sit at outdoor tables if you post the sign.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate.

shortcuts.name: Sell CBD lattes
shortcuts.what: A CBD shot adds $3 to a drink and a line on the chalkboard: about 1% more sales. The Health Department treats CBD in food and drinks as an unapproved additive: the product is embargoed and the fine runs $200 to $650.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate: a $3 add-on in one of every 35 orders.

shortcuts.name: Put off the water heater repair
shortcuts.what: The heater is dying and the hand sink runs lukewarm. A plumber costs money today; waiting saves about $120 a month. No hot water at the hand sink is 10 points, 28 if the whole shop is without it, and the inspector can close you until it is fixed.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: a $1,400 repair or replacement put off for a year.

shortcuts.name: Leave the step at the door
shortcuts.what: A portable ramp, a bell, a lower counter section and a website a screen reader can use cost about $2,400. Skipping them saves $100 a month. Lawyers file thousands of these suits a year in New York, and settling one costs about $10,000 plus the fixes.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: $2,400 of readily achievable fixes spread over 24 months. A small business gets half of such spending back as a federal tax credit of up to $5,000 a year (IRS Form 8826).

shortcuts.name: Skip the harassment policy and training
shortcuts.what: No written policy, no yearly training: saves an hour of paid time per worker a year and some paperwork, about $5 per worker a month. The state requires both from every employer; without them you have no defense when a claim comes.
shortcuts.note: One paid hour at $17-$21 a year per worker plus the owner's time, rounded up to $5 a month; the state's model policy and training are free.

shortcuts.name: Stop carding at the bar
shortcuts.what: Only if you sell beer and wine. Carding every customer slows the evening line; skipping it adds about 0.5% to sales. The Liquor Authority sends underage decoys: $2,500 to $4,000 for a first sale, up to $10,000, then the license.
shortcuts.note: The 0.5% is my estimate. Makes sense only once the beer and wine module exists (extra.mechanics.beer_wine_module).

shortcuts.name: Let the health permit lapse
shortcuts.what: The Food Service Establishment Permit renews every year for $280. Forgetting or skipping it saves $23 a month. Serving without a current permit is $1,000, $2,000 if you ignore the summons, and grounds to close the shop the same day.
shortcuts.note: $280 / 12 = $23. In life this is almost always forgetfulness, not a plan: the renewal notice goes to an old email address.

violations.name: Letter grade card not posted, hidden or removed
violations.law: 24 RCNY §23-07; NYC Health Code §81.51; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, codes 20-05, 20-06, 20-07
violations.note: Appendix 23-C: code 20-06 grade card not posted $500 (default $1,000); code 20-05 card not conspicuously posted or not visible to passersby $500 (default $1,000); code 20-07 grade card removed, destroyed or defaced $1,000 (default $2,000). The game uses the removal row: $1,000, or $2,000 if the summons is ignored. Numbers read in search excerpts of the rule text; the page itself could not be opened from this session.

violations.name: Hand-wash sink blocked, without hot water, soap or paper towels
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.21; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 05D
violations.note: Appendix 23-A, code 05D (critical): no hand wash facility in or next to the toilet room or within 25 feet of food preparation, facility blocked or used for something else, no hot and cold running water, no soap or drying device: 10 points at condition IV and 28 points at condition V, which alone is a C. Appendix 23-C penalty $300 to $350. The one closure day is my estimate: with no hot water in the shop at all the inspector cannot let service continue until it is back.

violations.name: Ready-to-eat food handled with bare hands
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.07; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04C
violations.note: Penalty schedule, code 04C, a public health hazard: food worker does not use a utensil or other barrier to avoid bare hand contact with ready-to-eat food: $250, $300, $350, $400 and $600 by condition level, the level set by the number of workers doing it. A pastry picked up without tongs, tissue or gloves counts. Game formula: $300 in the first month up to $600.

violations.name: Dogs or other live animals inside the shop
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.25; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04O
violations.note: Penalty schedule, code 04O (critical): live animal other than fish in a tank or a service animal present in the food or non-food areas: $200, $200, $250, $300, $350 by the number of animals. Service animals must be let in; a pet dog may sit only at outdoor tables under the city's dogs-in-outdoor-dining rules.

violations.name: Refusing or obstructing a health inspection
violations.law: NYC Health Code §3.15(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 07A
violations.note: Appendix 23-C, code 07A: obstruction of Department personnel $1,000 (seen in the rule excerpt). The $2,000 ceiling is my assumption that the default penalty doubles, as it does for the grade card rows; the default figure was not in the excerpt. Locking the door, hiding the kitchen or keeping the inspector waiting all count, and the inspection then happens anyway.

violations.name: Fire extinguishers missing, blocked or not serviced
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 906; 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 1
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 1 (portable fire extinguishers and fire hoses): first violation $600, mitigated to $300 if you appear at the hearing and prove it was fixed by the hearing date, $1,000 if you default; second violation $1,500 (mitigated $750, maximum $5,000). FDNY's portable extinguisher flyer: extinguishers must be serviced yearly by a company holding an FDNY certificate (W-96) and checked visually every month, with the tag dated and initialed. Fire Code section number cited from memory.

violations.name: Exit door or exit path blocked
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 1031 (maintenance of means of egress); 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 9
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 9 (rooftop access and means of egress): first violation $950, mitigated $475, $1,000 on default; second violation $2,375 (mitigated $1,185, maximum $5,000). Milk crates, cup cases and the mop bucket in the back corridor are the usual cause in a small shop. Fire Code section number cited from memory.

violations.name: Overcrowding: more people than the space is approved for
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 107.6; NYC Administrative Code §28-117.1 (Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation for 75 or more people); 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 10
violations.note: FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 10 (overcrowding): first violation $950, mitigated $475, $1,000 on default; second violation $2,375 (mitigated $1,185, maximum $5,000). The game charges $950 the first time and caps at the second-violation amount. A room that gathers 75 or more people needs a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (NYC Business restaurant page); a small cafe has none, so a packed open-mic night breaks the rule. Fire Code and Administrative Code section numbers cited from memory. Fire officers can also order the room emptied on the spot.

violations.name: Candles or open flame without an FDNY permit
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 105.6, FC 308; 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 3
violations.note: FDNY Restaurant Fire Safety Guide (2026 edition): open flames such as candles in a dining area need an FDNY permit; the yearly inspection fee is $210. FDNY penalty schedule, Violation Category 3 (permits): first violation $700, mitigated $350, $1,000 on default; second violation $1,750. Fire Code section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Construction, plumbing or electrical work without a Buildings permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1, §28-213.1 (civil penalty for work without a permit)
violations.note: Department of Buildings: for buildings other than one- and two-family homes the civil penalty for work without a permit is 21 times the permit fee, never less than $6,000 and never more than $15,000; the inspector also posts a Stop Work Order, and working through it costs $6,000 for the first offense. The work must then be legalized with filed plans, so the permit is paid for anyway. Numbers read in search excerpts of DOB pages and service notices; the section numbers are cited from memory.

violations.name: Working through a Stop Work Order
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-207.2 (stop work orders)
violations.criminal: Violating a Stop Work Order is also a misdemeanor under the Administrative Code (§28-207.2, cited from memory).
violations.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings Stop Work Order page: first offense $6,000. The amount for later offenses was not in the excerpt (from memory it is $12,000); the game charges $6,000 for every month the work goes on. The order stays on the door until the permit exists and the penalties are paid.

violations.name: Sidewalk and gutter not swept
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118(2)
violations.note: DSNY guide for businesses, Avoiding Common Sanitation Violations: failure to clean the sidewalk $100 to $300; failure to clean 18 inches from the curb into the street $100 to $300 (two separate tickets). Sanitation agents may ticket a commercial property only during two one-hour periods a day, printed on the DSNY notice for the block. Game formula: $100 the first month, up to $300.

violations.name: Shop trash in public litter baskets, no private carter
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-116 (commercial waste must go to a licensed private carter), §16-120(c) and (e)
violations.note: DSNY guide for businesses: every business must hire a private carter and post its decal; business waste may never be placed in or beside the corner litter baskets; fine $100 to $300 (Administrative Code §16-120(c) and (e)). Game formula: $100 plus $100 for each further month, capped at $300 per ticket. Agents open the bags and look for mail and receipts with the shop's name. §16-116 cited from memory.

violations.name: A-frame sign or merchandise blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118 and §19-136 (sidewalk obstructions)
violations.note: NYC311: a sandwich or A-frame sign may not reach more than 3 feet into the sidewalk from the building. The Sanitation Department told the Midtown Gazette in 2015 that the fine is $100 for a first sign violation and up to $300 after that; a New York coffee shop was reported fined $300 for a sidewalk sign. I did not find the current penalty row, so the amounts are from press reports. Section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Backflow prevention device not tested this year
violations.law: 15 RCNY §20-04(e); NYS Sanitary Code 10 NYCRR §5-1.31
violations.note: OATH water penalty schedule: failure to submit the annual backflow test report (15 RCNY §20-04(e)) $500, mitigated to $50 if the report is filed before the first hearing date, $1,000 maximum. The device on the water service must be tested once a year by a state-certified tester and the report sent to the Department of Environmental Protection, which finds missing reports from its own records. In 2018 the city wrote 8,780 violations for missing reports (Public Advocate). The state code section is cited from memory.

violations.name: Music too loud for the neighbors
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §24-231(a) (commercial music); 15 RCNY §47-02 (Noise Code penalty schedule)
violations.note: Noise Code: music from a commercial establishment may not exceed 42 dB(A) measured inside a neighbor's home. Penalty schedule for §24-231(a): $2,000 for a first offense, $4,000 for a second, $6,000 for a third; maximums $8,000, $16,000 and $24,000. A Department of Environmental Protection form lets a first offender bring the $2,000 down to $0 by admitting the violation and filing proof of correction from a noise consultant by the deadline. Found through 311 complaints: an inspector takes a reading in the complainant's apartment.

violations.name: Card surcharge not shown in the posted price
violations.law: NY General Business Law §518
violations.note: General Business Law §518 as in force since February 11, 2024: a seller who adds a credit card surcharge must post the highest total price including the surcharge, and the surcharge may not be more than what the card processor charges the seller; civil penalty up to $500 per violation, enforced by local consumer agencies. A sign that says '3% fee on cards' next to a single menu price does not comply; two posted prices (cash and card) do. The rule covers credit cards, not debit cards.

violations.name: Required health signs and posters missing
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-172 (choking first aid poster), §17-188 (resuscitation equipment); NYC Health Code §81.21(c) (wash hands sign); NYC Health Code Article 81 (Healthy Eating Information poster)
violations.note: Seen at NYC Health: restaurants must post the choking first aid poster, the CPR equipment notice, the wash-hands sign, the no smoking sign and the Healthy Eating Information poster (alcohol and pregnancy warning if alcohol is served); the city gives all of them away free through 311. Seen: $200 for a missing Healthy Eating poster (NYC Health FAQ) and $200 for a missing wash-hands sign (2022 rule notice). The $200 per sign and the three-sign cap of $600 are my simplification; the penalty rows for the choking poster and the CPR kit were not in any excerpt I could read. Sign violations are unscored and many can be cured for $0 the first time (Local Law 80 of 2021). Section numbers 17-188 and 81.21(c) as cited by the sources.

violations.name: No food allergy notice on the menu, no allergen labels on packed food
violations.law: NY Public Health Law §1356 (allergy notice) and §1357 (allergen labels on food packed on the premises, in force since November 12, 2026); NYC Administrative Code §17-195
violations.note: NYC Health: New York State requires restaurants to post a food allergies and intolerances sign where all food workers can see it, in the languages they speak, and to print an allergy statement on menus, online menus included; beginning January 2027 a restaurant that does not comply may receive a summons with a $100 fine. Public Health Law §1356 caps the civil penalty at $125 per violation. §1357 (allergen labels on food made, packed and sold in the same shop) names no penalty of its own; the game uses the same row for it. The fine is small; the real exposure is an allergic reaction with no notice and no label (extra.lawsuits).

violations.name: Trash set out in bags, at the wrong time, or without a lidded bin
violations.law: 16 RCNY §1-02.1 (commercial containerization); NYC Administrative Code §16-120
violations.note: Sanitation Department: since March 1, 2024 every business must put trash at the curb in bins with secure lids; $50 for a first offense, $100 for a second, $200 for every one after. DSNY business set-out rules: bins go out one hour before closing or after 8 PM and must be back inside by the time the shop reopens. Game formula follows the three steps. The rule section number is cited from memory.

violations.name: Foam cups or containers
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-329
violations.note: Sanitation Department: single-use foam cups, plates, trays and clamshells have been banned since January 1, 2019; fines for each notice within 12 months are $150 for the first offense, $250 for the second and $500 for the third and later. The Health Department and DCWP inspectors can write the same violation.

violations.name: Plastic straws and utensils handed out without being asked
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-401 (plastic straws, Local Law 64 of 2021) and §16-402 (utensils, condiments and napkins only on request, Local Law 17 of 2023)
violations.note: NYC311 plastic straw rules: plastic straws only on request, with a sign at any self-serve station; $100 for a first violation, $200 for a second and $400 for a third within 12 months; enforced since November 1, 2022. Sanitation Department: utensils, condiment packets, napkins and extra containers may go into a takeout or delivery order only if the customer asks; $50, $150 and $250; violations written since July 1, 2024. The game uses the straw schedule. Section numbers and the local law number for utensils are cited from memory.

violations.name: Playing music without a public performance license
violations.law: 17 U.S.C. §§106(4), 501, 504(c); 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B) (narrow exemption for radio and TV broadcasts in a food or drinking place under 3,750 sq ft)
violations.note: Not a government fine: the licensing societies (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR) send letters, then a field agent notes the songs played, then they sue in federal court. Copyright law sets statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song and up to $150,000 if willful, plus the other side's legal fees. Seen in press: four Connecticut judgments against restaurants averaged just over $3,600 a song; a Massachusetts bar paid $15,000 for five songs; a Connecticut restaurant $18,000 for nine. Game formula is my estimate: four songs at the $750 minimum ($3,000) plus $500 for each month the letters were ignored, capped at $30,000. A personal Spotify or Apple Music account is not licensed for a business; the radio exemption does not cover streaming.

violations.name: No sexual harassment policy or yearly training
violations.law: NY Labor Law §201-g, §218; NYC Administrative Code §8-107(29)
violations.note: Labor Law §201-g: every employer, whatever its size, must adopt a written sexual harassment prevention policy at least as strong as the state model and give every employee interactive training every year. The section sets no fine of its own. Game formula uses Labor Law §218 for violations other than unpaid wages, as quoted in the research notes: up to $1,000 for a first violation, $2,000 for a second, $3,000 for a third. The larger cost is in court: with no policy and no training an employer loses its main defense in a harassment claim.

violations.name: Storefront sign or awning installed without a permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1, §28-213.1; NYC Zoning Resolution sign rules; Local Law 28 of 2019
violations.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: a sign larger than 6 square feet needs a permit, and work without a permit on a commercial building is fined at 21 times the permit fee, never less than $6,000 and never more than $15,000. An appeals court upheld a $6,000 fine for an awning sign hung without a permit, and CBS reported $5,000 sign fines in 2018-2019 after a wave of 311 complaints against whole avenues. Local Law 28 of 2019 then froze penalties for business signs up to 150 sq ft and 1,200 lb; as I read it, the relief covers signs that already existed in February 2019, not a new sign, and I could not confirm whether DOB still applies it in 2026. Game formula: the $6,000 floor.

violations.name: CBD or another unapproved additive in drinks
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05 (adulterated food), §81.07
violations.note: Press reports from 2019 (CBS New York, Fox Business, Hemp Industry Daily): the Health Department barred restaurants and cafes from adding CBD to food or drinks, first embargoing the product on the shelf and, from October 1, 2019, writing fines of $200 to $650 by quantity; an earlier embargo hit activated charcoal. I did not find a 2026 city page confirming the amounts, so the range is from the press. Health Code section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Smoking or vaping allowed; no signs, no written policy
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-503, §17-508 (Smoke-Free Air Act)
violations.note: NYC Health: smoking and e-cigarette use are banned in restaurants, outdoor dining areas included; the owner must post no smoking and no vaping signs and keep a written smoking policy for staff. Penalties as described in the text of the 2002 act: $200 to $400 for a first violation, $500 to $1,000 for a second within 12 months, $1,000 to $2,000 for a third. I did not see the current penalty row, so the amounts are marked as an estimate. Section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Workers' rights poster not posted or handed out
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §32-102 (Local Law 161 of 2023)
violations.note: Law-firm alerts on Local Law 161 of 2023: since July 1, 2024 every NYC employer must post the city's 'Your Rights at Work' poster where staff can see it and give a copy to each worker, new hires on their first day; a first violation gets 30 days to cure, after that the civil penalty is $500. The statute itself was not opened, so this is marked as an estimate.

violations.name: Punishing a worker who complained
violations.law: NY Labor Law §215
violations.note: Labor Law §215: an employer may not fire, threaten or penalize a worker for complaining about pay or working conditions, to the boss or to the state. The Commissioner may assess a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000 (up to $20,000 with a prior violation in six years) and order reinstatement and lost pay; a court shall award liquidated damages of up to $20,000 to each worker. The worker has two years to sue (NYS DOL). Game formula: the $10,000 top of the first-violation penalty; with liquidated damages the total reaches $30,000. Cutting shifts or hours after a complaint counts.

violations.name: Job ad without a pay range
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §8-107(32); NY Labor Law §194-b
violations.note: NYC Human Rights Law: an employer with four or more workers must state the minimum and maximum pay in every job ad, a note in the window or an Instagram story included; the Commission can fine up to $250,000, but a first violation costs $0 if cured within 30 days. State Labor Law §194-b (in force since September 17, 2023): civil penalties up to $3,000. Game formula is my estimate: $1,000, capped at the state maximum. The city Commission also sends testers who answer ads.

violations.name: Step at the door, no ramp, website a screen reader cannot use
violations.law: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III (42 U.S.C. §12182); NYC Administrative Code §8-107(4); NY Executive Law §296(2)
violations.note: Not a city fine: a private lawsuit. Seyfarth Shaw counted 8,667 federal ADA Title III lawsuits in 2025, of them 3,117 about websites, with New York the busiest state for website suits (1,021). NY1 reported an East Harlem restaurant sued over an 8-inch step with 43 alleged violations, and plaintiffs who each filed more than 100 suits; each suit asks for about $1,000 in damages plus the plaintiff's legal fees and an order to fix the barrier. The federal law gives no damages, but the city and state human rights laws do, and the loser pays the winner's lawyer. The $10,000 settlement-plus-lawyers figure and the $25,000 cap are my estimate: no public statistic of settlements exists because they are confidential. A complaint to the city Commission on Human Rights can instead end in a civil penalty of up to $125,000 (Administrative Code §8-126, cited from memory).

violations.name: Beer or wine sold to someone under 21
violations.law: NY Alcoholic Beverage Control Law §65, §17(3)
violations.criminal: The person who makes the sale can be arrested and charged with a misdemeanor.
violations.note: State Liquor Authority press releases on 2026 underage compliance checks: licensees charged with underage sales face civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, with fines starting at $2,500 to $4,000 for a first offense; repeat offenders face suspension or revocation of the license. The Authority sends underage decoys with investigators. The licensee answers even if an employee made the sale and even if the buyer looked 21 or lied (SLA Handbook for Retail Licensees, July 2025). Applies only to a cafe that holds a beer and wine license. ABC Law section numbers cited from memory.

officials.name: Fire inspector
officials.realProcess: Fire inspectors and local firehouse companies walk through businesses unannounced and answer 311 complaints. They check extinguisher tags, exit paths, extension cords and permits, then write a violation order to fix it or a summons to the city tribunal (OATH), where the fine is halved if you prove the fix before the hearing.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Almost always sent by a 311 complaint: a neighbor hears demolition or sees a dumpster and no permit in the window. The inspector posts a Stop Work Order and writes a summons to OATH. The work must be legalized with filed plans before the order is lifted.

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Agents walk commercial streets on a route. For dirty sidewalks they may ticket a shop only during two posted one-hour windows a day; for trash set out wrong, missing carter decals, foam cups and sidewalk obstructions they ticket at any time. Tickets are answered at OATH.

officials.name: Environmental inspector
officials.realProcess: Three separate units: sewer inspectors open the grease interceptor and ask for cleaning records; the cross-connection unit mails a notice when the yearly backflow test report is missing; noise inspectors answer 311 complaints and take a decibel reading inside the neighbor's home.

officials.name: Civil court (private lawsuits)
officials.agency: U.S. District Court (S.D.N.Y. and E.D.N.Y.) and New York State Supreme Court
officials.realProcess: Not an inspector: a private party's lawyer files a complaint and a process server hands you the summons. Small businesses almost always settle within months, because the law makes the loser pay the other side's legal fees and a defense costs more than the settlement.

officials.name: Human rights investigator
officials.realProcess: The Commission takes complaints from the public and runs its own tests: testers answer job ads and visit businesses. Small employers are usually offered an early resolution: fix it, train the staff and pay a set penalty. A contested case goes to the city tribunal (OATH).

officials.name: Liquor Authority investigator
officials.realProcess: Investigators send underage decoys into licensed places and watch the sale. Charges go to a hearing before the Authority, which can fine, suspend or revoke the license. Only a cafe with a beer and wine license ever meets them.

officials.name: Health inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
officials.realProcess: Unannounced, at least once a year. The inspector walks the whole shop with a thermometer and a flashlight and scores each violation in points: under 14 is an A, and an A on the first visit also means no fines for the scored violations. With 14 or more, a second inspection comes about a month later and sets the grade; with 28 or more, inspectors keep coming about once a month. A hazard that cannot be fixed on the spot closes the shop. Fines are decided afterwards at the city tribunal (OATH).

reports.name: Report a fire hazard (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint routed to the Fire Department. Fire inspectors check extinguisher tags, exits, crowding and open-flame permits. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report construction or a sign without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Department of Buildings. An inspector looks for the permit in the window and can post a Stop Work Order the same day. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a dirty sidewalk or trash set out wrong (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Sanitation Department. An agent checks the sidewalk and gutter, the bins and lids, the carter's decal, foam cups and anything blocking the sidewalk. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report loud music (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 noise complaint. An inspector from Environmental Protection takes a decibel reading inside the neighbor's home; over 42 decibels is a violation. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a missing grade card, a pet inside or bare-hand food handling (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about a food establishment. A health inspector checks the grade card in the window, the required signs, the hand sinks and how food is handled. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report getting sick after eating there (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 foodborne illness complaint. The Health Department interviews the person who got sick and sends an inspector to check temperatures, hand washing and where the food came from. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a hidden card fee or refused cash (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 consumer complaint to the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. An inspector compares the posted prices with the receipt and tries to pay in cash. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a missing backflow test or grease in the sewer (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to Environmental Protection. The department checks its records for the yearly backflow test report and sends an inspector to open the grease interceptor. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a barrier for disabled customers or an illegal job ad (Human Rights Commission)
reports.text: In real life: a complaint to the NYC Commission on Human Rights, which can also send testers. It checks the entrance, the service and the wording of help-wanted ads. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report retaliation or missing workplace notices (NYS Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a labor standards complaint, often filed by a former worker. An investigator asks who complained, what happened to their shifts, and for the harassment policy, training records and required posters. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Tip off a music licensing society
reports.text: In real life: ASCAP, BMI and SESAC take tips and send field agents who sit in the shop and write down the songs. No license means letters, then a federal lawsuit. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report alcohol sold to minors (State Liquor Authority)
reports.text: In real life: a complaint to the State Liquor Authority, which sends an underage decoy with an investigator. Works only against a shop that holds a beer and wine license. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

ruleCards.title: How points add up
ruleCards.text: Inspectors score each violation by how bad it is: general ones 2-5 points, critical ones 5-10, public health hazards 7 or more, and 28 at the worst level. A total under 14 is an A, 14-27 a B, 28 or more a C.

ruleCards.title: An A means no fines
ruleCards.text: Score under 14 points on an initial inspection and you pay no fines for the scored violations found that day. Signs, smoking and other unscored violations are still fined.

ruleCards.title: Grade Pending
ruleCards.text: Score 14 or more on a re-inspection and the B or C is not final until your hearing. Until then you may post the 'Grade Pending' card the inspector leaves instead of the letter.

ruleCards.title: After a 28
ruleCards.text: Score 28 or more and inspectors keep coming about once a month until you score under 28, or until the Health Department closes the shop for serious and persistent violations.

ruleCards.title: Practice inspection from the city
ruleCards.text: The Health Department sells practice inspections: $100 for a new restaurant before its first graded visit, $400 after. No violations are written, but a public health hazard must still be fixed on the spot.

ruleCards.title: Closed by the Health Department
ruleCards.text: Inspectors close a shop for a hazard that cannot be fixed during the visit, or for no permit. One tracker counted 583 closures at 518 NYC restaurants in a year, about 2.5% of those inspected; mice were cited in 44%.

ruleCards.title: Tickets go to a hearing
ruleCards.text: City tickets are decided at OATH, the city tribunal. You can pay, accept the agency's settlement offer, or contest by phone, online or mail. For fire tickets, proof of the fix by the hearing date halves the fine: $600 becomes $300.

ruleCards.title: Never skip a hearing
ruleCards.text: Miss the hearing and you lose by default at the higher penalty: a $500 grade-card ticket becomes $1,000. Unpaid defaults become court judgments handed to the sheriff or a city marshal. You get one request to reopen.

ruleCards.title: Fix it and pay $0
ruleCards.text: For some first-time violations that are not food-safety hazards, such as a missing sign, the city lets you fix the problem within days, notify the agency and pay $0 (Local Law 80 of 2021).

ruleCards.title: The card stays in the window
ruleCards.text: The grade card must hang where people walking by can see it. No card: $500, or $1,000 if you skip the hearing. Removing, hiding or faking it: $1,000, or $2,000. Every card has a serial number.

ruleCards.title: Hand sinks
ruleCards.text: Every hand sink needs hot and cold water, soap and paper towels, and must stay clear. A dead hand sink is 10 points; at the worst level it is 28 points, a C by itself, and the inspector can close you until it works.

ruleCards.title: No bare hands
ruleCards.text: Food that is ready to eat may not be touched with bare hands: use tongs, tissue or gloves for every pastry and garnish. It is a public health hazard: $250 to $600 per citation.

ruleCards.title: Dogs
ruleCards.text: Pet dogs may not come inside a food shop: $200-$350 and a critical violation. Service dogs must be allowed wherever customers go, tag or no tag. Pets may sit at outdoor tables only if you opt in and post the sign.

ruleCards.title: Let the inspector in
ruleCards.text: Refusing or delaying a health inspection costs $1,000, and the inspection still happens. One owner who refused an inspection as a protest had his restaurant closed by the Health Department.

ruleCards.title: Signs on the wall
ruleCards.text: Restaurants must post the choking first aid poster, the CPR kit notice, hand-wash signs, no smoking signs and the Healthy Eating poster. The city gives them away free through 311. A missing one costs about $200.

ruleCards.title: Allergy notice
ruleCards.text: New York requires an allergy notice on every menu, online menus too, and an allergy poster where staff can see it, in their languages. From January 2027 the city writes $100 summonses; state law allows up to $125.

ruleCards.title: Allergen labels on grab-and-go
ruleCards.text: Since November 12, 2026, food you make, pack and sell in the same shop for takeaway, such as a wrapped sandwich or a cup of overnight oats, needs a label naming its major allergens (Public Health Law §1357).

ruleCards.title: Extinguisher tags
ruleCards.text: Extinguishers need a yearly service by an FDNY-certified company and a quick check every month, dated and initialed on the tag. A missing or expired tag: $600, or $300 if you fix it and show proof at the hearing.

ruleCards.title: Keep the exit clear
ruleCards.text: Exit doors and the path to them must stay clear at all times. Boxes in the back corridor cost $950, or $475 if cleared before the hearing; a second ticket is $2,375.

ruleCards.title: How many people fit
ruleCards.text: A room that gathers 75 or more people needs a Place of Assembly certificate. Overcrowding a small cafe costs $950, then $2,375, and fire officers can clear the room in the middle of your event.

ruleCards.title: Candles
ruleCards.text: Candles on restaurant tables need an FDNY open flame permit: $210 a year. Without it: $700, or $350 if you get the permit before the hearing.

ruleCards.title: Permits before the hammer
ruleCards.text: Moving plumbing, adding outlets or building walls needs a Buildings permit. Work without one costs 21 times the permit fee, at least $6,000 and up to $15,000, plus a Stop Work Order; working through the order is another $6,000.

ruleCards.title: The sign needs a permit too
ruleCards.text: A sign over 6 square feet needs a Buildings permit and a licensed installer. One 311 complaint can bring a work-without-a-permit fine of $6,000. In 2018-2019 whole avenues of shop signs were reported at once.

ruleCards.title: Your sidewalk, your broom
ruleCards.text: You must sweep your sidewalk and 18 inches into the street. Each is a separate ticket of $100 to $300. Sanitation agents may ticket a business for this only during two set one-hour windows a day.

ruleCards.title: Bins with lids
ruleCards.text: Since March 2024 business trash goes to the curb in bins with secure lids, one hour before closing or after 8 PM, and the bins come back in by opening time. $50, then $100, then $200 every time after.

ruleCards.title: Not in the corner basket
ruleCards.text: Shop trash may never go into public litter baskets or the building's residential pile. You must hire a private carter and post its decal. Agents open bags and look for your receipts: $100 to $300.

ruleCards.title: A-frame signs
ruleCards.text: An A-frame sign may stand no more than 3 feet from your wall. Farther out it is a sidewalk obstruction: about $100 the first time and up to $300 after.

ruleCards.title: Foam, straws and forks
ruleCards.text: Foam cups and containers are banned: $150, then $250, then $500. Plastic straws only on request: $100 to $400. Forks, napkins and sauce packets go into takeout only if the customer asks: $50 to $250.

ruleCards.title: Backflow test
ruleCards.text: The backflow valve on your water line must be tested every year by a certified tester and the report sent to the city. A missing report: $500, cut to $50 if you file it before the hearing, $1,000 if you ignore the ticket.

ruleCards.title: 42 decibels
ruleCards.text: Music from a business may not exceed 42 decibels inside a neighbor's home. First violation $2,000, then $4,000, then $6,000. A first offender who fixes it and files a noise consultant's report can have the $2,000 cut to $0.

ruleCards.title: Card fees must be posted
ruleCards.text: You may add a credit card surcharge only if the full card price is posted and the fee is no more than your processing cost. A surprise fee at the register: up to $500 per violation. Debit cards cannot be surcharged.

ruleCards.title: No extra percentages on the menu
ruleCards.text: A place serving food to eat in may not add a percentage to listed prices: a 5% living-wage fee or a 20% administrative charge is illegal. Allowed if disclosed up front: a split-plate charge or a gratuity for parties of 8 or more.

ruleCards.title: Music needs a license
ruleCards.text: Music in a shop is a public performance, and a personal streaming account is not a license. Copyright law allows $750 to $30,000 per song; restaurant judgments have averaged about $3,600 a song.

ruleCards.title: Harassment policy and training
ruleCards.text: Every New York employer, even with 1 worker, needs a written sexual harassment prevention policy and interactive training for every worker every year. The state publishes a free model policy and training.

ruleCards.title: Free posters, real duty
ruleCards.text: NYC employers must post the city's 'Your Rights at Work' poster and hand a copy to every worker on day one. First miss: 30 days to fix. After that: $500. Official posters are free; mailers asking $92.58 for one are a scam.

ruleCards.title: No payback for complaints
ruleCards.text: You may not fire, threaten or cut the hours of a worker who complains about pay or safety. The state can fine $1,000 to $10,000, and a court awards the worker up to $20,000 more, plus lost pay.

ruleCards.title: Pay range in every job ad
ruleCards.text: An employer with 4 or more workers must show a pay range in every job ad, even an Instagram post. NYC lets you fix a first violation within 30 days for $0; after that fines run up to $250,000. The state adds up to $3,000.

ruleCards.title: Access lawsuits
ruleCards.text: Lawyers filed 8,667 federal disability-access suits in 2025; New York led in website suits with 1,021. A step at the door or a site a screen reader cannot use is enough. Half of what you spend on fixes returns as a tax credit, up to $5,000 a year.

ruleCards.title: No rent control for shops
ruleCards.text: New York has no commercial rent control and no right to renew a store lease. At renewal the landlord may ask any rent: in 2025 one Brooklyn cafe's rent nearly tripled and another faced $4,000 more a month. Both closed.

ruleCards.title: If you miss the rent
ruleCards.text: The landlord must first serve a written 14-day demand. Then comes a court case; after a judgment a city marshal gives 14 days' notice before changing the locks. Paying everything owed before that stops the eviction.

ruleCards.title: Landlord harassment
ruleCards.text: A landlord may refuse to renew, but may not force you out by cutting services or blocking your door. Commercial tenant harassment carries a civil penalty of $10,000 to $50,000, and you can sue.

ruleCards.title: No smoking, no vaping
ruleCards.text: No smoking or vaping inside or at your outdoor tables. Post the signs and keep a written policy. Fines for the owner: $200-$400 the first time, $500-$1,000 the second, $1,000-$2,000 the third.

ruleCards.title: CBD in drinks
ruleCards.text: New York City's Health Department does not allow CBD added to food or drinks in restaurants and cafes: inspectors embargo the product, and fines have run $200 to $650.

ruleCards.title: Beer, wine and decoys
ruleCards.text: A beer and wine license brings the Liquor Authority, which sends underage decoys. A first sale to a minor costs $2,500 to $4,000, up to $10,000 per violation, and repeats can cost the license.

ruleCards.title: Real inspectors do not take cash
ruleCards.text: Real city inspectors show photo ID and never take money on the spot: fines are paid to the city after a hearing. Anyone asking for cash for an inspection, a $92.58 poster or an extinguisher check is running a scam.

ruleCards.title: Hot drinks burn
ruleCards.text: In 2025 a Los Angeles jury awarded $50 million to a delivery driver burned when a hot tea was not secured in its carrier. Lids pressed on, cups seated in the tray and a liability policy are cheap by comparison.

ruleCards.title: Slips and falls
ruleCards.text: Customer slip-and-falls are among the 5 most common restaurant insurance claims and often settle for $10,000 to $50,000. Mats at the door, wet-floor signs and a dated mopping log are what your insurer's lawyer asks for.

ruleCards.title: Anyone can call 311
ruleCards.text: Anyone can file a 311 complaint, without a name, and agencies send inspectors. A 2026 City Council bill would stop inspections after 3 unverified anonymous complaints in 6 months; it has not passed.

ruleCards.title: Wage suits come late and large
ruleCards.text: Wage claims reach back 6 years and usually arrive after a worker leaves. NYC restaurant wage suits settled for $725,000 to $1.75 million in 2025; Starbucks paid $35.5 million to about 15,000 city workers plus $3.4 million in penalties.

ruleCards.title: Waste zones keep rolling out
ruleCards.text: On October 16, 2026 four more commercial waste zones took effect: Brooklyn East, Manhattan Northeast, Queens West and Manhattan West. Inside a zone you may sign only with one of its 3 authorized carters.

ruleCards.title: Check the name first
ruleCards.text: Search trademarks before you print the name. A Michigan cafe sued by a national coffee chain was told a court fight could cost $50,000; it renamed for about $5,000. Another owner got 10 days to destroy branded goods.

ruleCards.title: Your grade follows you online
ruleCards.text: Under a rule in force since November 15, 2025, delivery apps must link to the city's inspection lookup. A B or C is now one tap away from your menu, not only in the window.

roadmap.title: Look up the building before you sign
roadmap.text: Search the address in the Buildings Department's public records. Open violations and Stop Work Orders on the building can hold up your own permits, and the Certificate of Occupancy must allow an eating and drinking place on your floor.

roadmap.title: Read the lease for what happens later
roadmap.text: There is no rent control for shops. Ask for a renewal option with a stated rent formula, a cap on yearly increases and on your share of real estate tax, a holdover rate, and clear words on who pays for the sidewalk, the backflow test and building violations.

roadmap.title: Search the name before you print it
roadmap.text: Search the federal trademark database and the state business records for your shop's name and anything close to it. Renaming after a lawyer's letter costs thousands; fighting one costs tens of thousands.

roadmap.title: File for the sign permit
roadmap.text: A sign over 6 square feet needs a Buildings permit and a licensed sign hanger. File while the build-out is under way: a sign hung without a permit can cost $6,000 after a single 311 complaint.

roadmap.title: Make the door and the website usable for everyone
roadmap.text: A step at the entrance, a counter nobody in a wheelchair can reach, or a menu that exists only as a photo are the usual grounds for an access lawsuit. Fix what is readily achievable and claim the federal tax credit: half of the spending, up to $5,000 a year.

roadmap.title: Test the backflow device and file the report
roadmap.text: Hire a certified tester for the backflow valve on your water service and send the report to Environmental Protection. Repeat every year: the city tracks missing reports from its own files, and the fine is $500.

roadmap.title: Mount and tag the fire extinguishers
roadmap.text: Have an FDNY-certified company mount and tag your extinguishers, then initial the tag after a quick check every month. Keep the exit path clear from day one: no stock in the corridor.

roadmap.title: Order and post the required signs
roadmap.text: Call 311 for the free posters: choking first aid, CPR kit, food allergy, no smoking. Add hand-wash signs at every sink and keep a spot in the window for the grade card. All of it must be up before the first inspection.

roadmap.title: Put the allergy notice on every menu
roadmap.text: State law requires an allergy statement on each menu and on your online ordering page, and a poster for staff in their languages. If you wrap food made in the shop for takeaway, label its major allergens: required since November 12, 2026.
roadmap.agency: NYS Department of Health / NYC DOHMH

roadmap.title: Workplace posters, harassment policy, pay-range ads
roadmap.text: Before the first hire: download the free state, city and federal posters, adopt the state's model harassment policy, schedule the yearly training, and write job ads with a pay range. Hand every new worker the city's 'Your Rights at Work' notice on day one.
roadmap.agency: NYS Department of Labor; NYC DCWP

roadmap.title: License the music
roadmap.text: Sign up for a background music service made for businesses, or buy licenses from the performing rights societies. A personal streaming account is not licensed for a shop, and the societies do send agents.

roadmap.title: Book the city's practice inspection
roadmap.text: Once you are serving, and before your first graded inspection, ask 311 for a Restaurant Consultative Inspection: $100, no violations written. It shows you the shop through an inspector's eyes while mistakes are still free.

roadmap.title: Know what to do with a summons
roadmap.text: Every city ticket carries a hearing date at OATH. Decide who opens the mail and answers within the deadline: fix and prove it, settle, or contest. A missed hearing means the top penalty and, unpaid, a court judgment.
roadmap.agency: NYC Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH)

suppliers.what: A state-certified backflow prevention device tester, usually a licensed plumbing firm, who tests the valve once a year and files the report with the city
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the building's plumber or search licensed master plumbers who advertise backflow testing; confirm the tester's state certification before the visit
suppliers.examples: Licensed master plumbing firms in every borough offer it as a yearly service
suppliers.note: No official price list; $150-$350 a test is my estimate from advertised ranges.

suppliers.what: A company approved by the Fire Department whose technicians hold the W-96 certificate; it sells, mounts, tags and services extinguishers once a year
suppliers.whereToFind: The Fire Department publishes a list of approved portable fire extinguisher companies; never buy service from someone who walks in unannounced
suppliers.examples: Borough fire-safety companies that also service restaurant hood systems
suppliers.note: FDNY guide: yearly servicing must be done by a W-96 certificate holder working for an FDNY-approved company. Prices are my estimate: about $120 a year for two units.

suppliers.what: A background music subscription for businesses that includes the public performance licenses, or direct licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR
suppliers.whereToFind: Compare business music services online; if you want your own playlists or live music, contact the performing rights societies directly
suppliers.examples: Soundtrack, Pandora CloudCover, Rockbot, SiriusXM Music for Business
suppliers.note: Service names are well-known examples, not endorsements; prices of $17-$50 a month are from vendor comparison pages for 2026.

suppliers.what: A lawyer who knows restaurants: lease terms, summonses, wage rules, access lawsuits. Also registered representatives who appear at city hearings for a flat fee
suppliers.whereToFind: The city's Small Business Services office and the New York City Bar referral service; the city tribunal's own Help Center explains hearings for free
suppliers.examples: NYC Small Business Services legal assistance for commercial leases; OATH Help Center; NYC Bar Legal Referral Service
suppliers.note: OATH materials: a free Help Center and a small-business unit exist. Lawyer prices are not published; the pack's legal_help lever uses my estimate of $150 a month.

suppliers.what: A private consultant, often a former inspector, who runs a mock inspection with the city's own scoring sheet and trains the staff
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask other owners and the restaurant trade association; the Health Department sells its own consultative inspection through 311
suppliers.examples: Independent food safety consultants; the Health Department's Restaurant Consultative Inspection ($100 new, $400 after grading)
suppliers.note: City prices seen at NYC Health; private consultants at about $350 a visit are my estimate.

suppliers.what: A licensed sign hanger who files the sign permit and installs the sign; a sign shop alone cannot hang anything over 6 square feet
suppliers.whereToFind: Search the Buildings Department's license lookup for sign hangers and ask for the license number and insurance certificate
suppliers.examples: Licensed master and special sign hangers working with neighborhood sign shops
suppliers.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: bigger signs need a permit obtained by a licensed sign hanger. Prices are quotes.

suppliers.what: Portable ramps and door hardware, a carpenter for a lowered counter, and a web developer who can test the site with a screen reader
suppliers.whereToFind: Medical supply and ramp dealers, your contractor, and your website builder's accessibility checklist; keep receipts for the tax credit
suppliers.examples: Aluminum threshold and portable ramps; website builders' built-in accessibility checkers
suppliers.note: IRS: the Disabled Access Credit (Form 8826) is open to businesses with $1 million or less in revenue or no more than 30 full-time workers. Product prices are my estimates.

suppliers.what: Every required poster and notice: health signs from the city, labor posters from the state, city and federal agencies, the model harassment policy
suppliers.whereToFind: Call 311 for the health posters; download the rest from the agencies' own websites. Never pay a mailer that looks like a government invoice
suppliers.examples: NYC Health required signs; NYS Department of Labor posting requirements; DCWP 'Your Rights at Work' poster
suppliers.note: Free by design. BBB Scam Tracker shows a New York mailer demanding $92.58 for a workplace poster.

eventCatalog.name: The first graded inspection
eventCatalog.text: A health inspector walks in unannounced, during service, with a thermometer and a flashlight. Whatever is true in the shop this month is what gets scored.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Date the shop started serving: every NYC restaurant gets an unannounced inspection at least once a year, and a new one gets its first graded visit after it opens (it may open 22 days after applying even if no inspector has come)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: More than 38,000 food service inspections in fiscal year 2025 for about 29,000 restaurants (Health Department ombuds report and July 2025 press release)
eventCatalog.note: In life the day is unknown. In the game the visit is announced as 'within your first two months' and happens to every new shop, so it is not a dice roll. The 1.5 multiplier is a design value.

eventCatalog.name: Re-inspection: the visit that sets the grade
eventCatalog.text: You scored 14 or more. The inspector returns in about a month, and this score goes on the card in the window.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own initial inspection score: 14 points or more triggers a re-inspection no sooner than 7 days later, typically within a month
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows every initial inspection of 14 points or more; older city figures put A grades at 85-93% of restaurants after re-inspection
eventCatalog.note: Health Department FAQ and 24 RCNY Chapter 23: re-inspection after an initial score of 14 or more; until the hearing the shop may post Grade Pending. After a B the next cycle starts in 5-7 months, after a C in 3-5 months, after an A in 11-13 months.

eventCatalog.name: Inspectors every month
eventCatalog.text: A score of 28 or more puts the shop on a short leash: an inspector returns about once a month until the score drops under 28 or the shop is closed.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own score of 28 or more
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every restaurant that scores 28 or more
eventCatalog.note: Health Department FAQ: the Department may keep inspecting roughly once a month until the restaurant scores below 28 or is closed for serious and persistent violations. Duration is as long as the score stays at 28 or above; 3 is a placeholder.

eventCatalog.name: Closed by order of the Health Commissioner
eventCatalog.text: A hazard that could not be fixed during the visit: no hot water, sewage on the floor, an infestation, or no permit. A yellow sign goes on the door and stays until a re-opening inspection.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own open violations at the worst condition level (28 points) or no valid permit at the time of an inspection
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 583 closures at 518 restaurants between October 2025 and September 2026, about 2.5% of the 20,932 restaurants inspected; mice were cited in 44% of closures (tracker of city data)
eventCatalog.note: Follows from the player's own violations, never from chance. The 5 closure days and the 10% drop in demand for two months after re-opening are my estimates; closures are published by the city and picked up by neighborhood news sites. Rent, wages owed and spoilage continue while closed.

eventCatalog.name: Your grade is one tap from your menu
eventCatalog.text: Delivery apps must link every restaurant page to the city's inspection lookup. A B or C now costs delivery orders as well as walk-ins.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Health Department rule adopted October 16, 2025, in force November 15, 2025: delivery platforms must post a link to the Department's inspection lookup tool
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Permanent rule; affects only shops with a B, a C or Grade Pending
eventCatalog.note: The rule is real; the 10% loss of delivery orders for a shop without an A is my estimate. Applies only while the shop's grade is not an A.

eventCatalog.name: The city announces an enforcement sweep
eventCatalog.text: An agency says in advance what it will ticket and from which date: a warning month first, then fines. Everyone on the street gets the same notice.
eventCatalog.realSignal: An agency press release with a warning period and a start date for fines; example: lidded-bin rule for all businesses, warnings from March 1, 2024, fines from April 2024
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Several a year across agencies: bins (2024), utensils on request (warnings until July 1, 2024), plastic straws (enforced from November 1, 2022), allergy notices (summonses from January 2027)
eventCatalog.note: Fits the game's rule: announced a month ahead, the same for everyone. The 1.5 multiplier on inspections is a design value. The host picks which family of violations the sweep targets.

eventCatalog.name: Someone keeps calling 311 about you
eventCatalog.text: A neighbor or a rival files complaint after complaint. Each one brings an inspector. If the shop is clean, each visit costs an hour; if not, it finds what is there.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 service requests against the address, public on NYC Open Data
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Common enough that a 2026 Council bill (Intro 924) would bar inspections after three unverified anonymous complaints in six months; not passed
eventCatalog.note: In the game this is another player's 'report to the city', not an AI event. Proposed cap for the lead: three empty complaints against one address in six months and further ones are not sent (mechanic complaint_channels).

eventCatalog.name: Allergen labels become law
eventCatalog.text: From November 12, 2026 every item you make, pack and sell in the same shop for takeaway needs a label naming its major allergens.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NY Public Health Law §1357 (S.5381/A.6558A), signed November 2025, effective November 12, 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: One-time change of law; statewide, every food establishment whatever its size
eventCatalog.note: State law, modeled at city scale because every player is in New York. The 0.2% cost-of-goods effect is my estimate of label cost for a shop that packs a tenth of its food; it applies only with the printed-labels option.

eventCatalog.name: Allergy notice: summonses start in January
eventCatalog.text: The Health Department starts writing $100 summonses for a missing allergy sign or a menu without the allergy statement.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Health required-signs page: beginning January 2027 non-compliant food service establishments may receive a summons subject to a $100 fine
eventCatalog.realFrequency: One-time start of enforcement
eventCatalog.note: The legal move is the free poster and the menu statement (setup item allergen_menu_statement). The multiplier is a design value.

eventCatalog.name: Your block joins a commercial waste zone
eventCatalog.text: From the start date only the three carters authorized for your zone may pick up your trash. Your old contract ends; sign a new one and post the new decal.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DSNY adopted rule: Brooklyn East, Manhattan Northeast, Queens West and Manhattan West zones in force October 16, 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Each zone once; the rollout runs zone by zone from January 2025
eventCatalog.note: The legal move is signing with a zone carter at or under its maximum rate; the pack's waste line already carries the cost, and I found no figure for how prices change inside a zone, so there is no money effect. The illegal move is having no carter.

eventCatalog.name: Consumer inspectors check posted prices
eventCatalog.text: Inspectors compare the menu with the receipt: card fees not shown in the price, percentages added to the bill, cash refused.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DCWP inspection checklist for restaurant surcharges and its amended surcharge rule (adopted March 2026); state card-surcharge law in force since February 11, 2024
eventCatalog.realFrequency: DCWP patrols and answers 311 consumer complaints all year
eventCatalog.note: The legal alternative to a hidden fee is two posted prices, cash and card (General Business Law §518). The multiplier is a design value. card_only is the existing common shortcut.

eventCatalog.name: A process server brings an access lawsuit
eventCatalog.text: A plaintiff who uses a wheelchair, or a screen reader, sues over the step at your door or your website. The same lawyer has filed dozens like it this year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Federal ADA Title III filings: 8,667 in 2025, of them 3,117 website suits; New York first in website suits with 1,021
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 24 federal access suits a day nationwide in 2025; in New York a few plaintiffs file more than 100 suits each
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed for the engine: the suit arrives after six months with the shortcut skip_accessibility_fixes active. 8,667 / 365 = 23.7 suits a day. The $10,000 is my estimate of settlement plus both lawyers; settlements are confidential.

eventCatalog.name: Letters from the music licensing societies
eventCatalog.text: First a letter, then phone calls, then an agent who sits with a coffee and writes down the songs. A year of silence from you ends in federal court.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop plays music with no license on file at ASCAP, BMI or SESAC
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The societies canvass new businesses from public records; lawsuits against restaurants and bars are filed in batches every year
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: letters start in the third month of the personal_account option; the claim (violation unlicensed_music) lands in the twelfth. Switching to a licensed option before then ends it at no cost. Judgments averaged about $3,600 a song in four Connecticut cases.

eventCatalog.name: A customer falls and files a claim
eventCatalog.text: A wet floor at the door, no mat, no sign. Weeks later a lawyer's letter arrives. With insurance you pay the deductible and a higher premium; without it, the settlement.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Rain and snow days at the door plus the shop's own floor routine; slip-and-fall is among the five most frequent restaurant insurance claims (NEXT Insurance data, 2021-2024)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About one in eight restaurant claims (12.8% in a secondary summary of insurer data); settlements commonly $10,000 to $50,000
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: the claim arrives after three wet-season months with floor_safety set to 'nothing'. The $2,500 is my estimate of a deductible plus the premium increase for an insured shop; an uninsured shop pays the settlement ($10,000 to $50,000, secondary source). A $575,000 settlement for a fall in a Brooklyn restaurant shows the tail.

eventCatalog.name: A customer has an allergic reaction
eventCatalog.text: Oat milk steamed in the dairy pitcher, a pastry with no label. The customer goes to the emergency room, then to a lawyer, and files a complaint with 311.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop has no allergy notice, no allergen labels or handles ready-to-eat food carelessly
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found for cafes; New York answered with two laws: allergy notices on menus (§1356) and allergen labels on food packed on site (§1357, November 2026)
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: arrives after six months with allergen_labels set to 'name_only' or with the allergy notice missing. No settlement figure was found, so the event carries an inspection and a 3% demand dip (my estimate) instead of a cash amount.

eventCatalog.name: A customer reports getting sick
