eventCatalog.text: Someone who ate at your shop calls 311. The Health Department interviews them and sends an inspector within days, looking at temperatures, hand washing and where the food came from.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own open trails: old food kept for sale, warm milk, food from a home kitchen, dirty surfaces
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found: the city takes foodborne illness complaints through 311 and publishes outbreak data, but I found no yearly count
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: arrives in a warm month once spoiled_food or unapproved_food_source has been open for two months. The 5% demand dip is my estimate. Warm months are chosen because cold-holding failures grow with heat; that link is my assumption.

eventCatalog.name: A worker who left files a wage claim
eventCatalog.text: Claims are filed after the job ends. The investigator asks for six years of time and pay records for everyone, not only the one who complained.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A worker leaves a shop that has any open wage trail: kept tips, unpaid training, unpaid overtime, off-the-clock work
eventCatalog.realFrequency: NYC restaurant wage suits settled for $725,000, $900,000 and $1.75 million in 2025; a coffee chain paid $35.5 million to about 15,000 city workers
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: when the head count drops while a wage shortcut is active, the audit is triggered the next month. Choosing 'cut_their_shifts' in the worker_complaints lever adds the retaliation case on top.

eventCatalog.name: A lawyer's letter about your name
eventCatalog.text: A bigger company says your name or logo is too close to theirs. They give you days to stop using it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop skipped the trademark search at opening
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Rare for one shop; reported every year somewhere: a Michigan cafe renamed for about $5,000 against $50,000 to fight, another owner got 10 days to destroy branded goods
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: only for a shop that did not buy the setup item trademark_search_and_filing. The $5,000 is the reported cost of renaming; the 3% demand dip while regulars find the new name is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: A man with a clipboard wants cash
eventCatalog.text: He says he is from the Fire Department and your extinguishers failed; pay now for the service or get a summons. Real inspectors show photo ID and never take money.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Scam alerts from fire and health departments; impostors work a whole street in a day
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Recurring: fire officials in Yonkers warned businesses about fake extinguisher inspectors; the city's investigators once caught a consultant selling fake A grade cards to restaurants
eventCatalog.note: Hits the whole block the same month; only shops whose staff instruction is 'pay_whoever_asks' lose money. The $350 is my estimate of a fake service bill. Paying a real inspector instead would be bribery (common violation).

eventCatalog.name: An official-looking invoice for a labor poster
eventCatalog.text: A mailer with a seal and a deadline demands $92.58 for a 'mandatory workplace poster'. The real posters are free on the agencies' websites.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New business registrations are public; mailers follow every new filing and every January wage change
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reported to the Better Business Bureau from New York; arrives soon after a business registers
eventCatalog.note: The amount is from the BBB Scam Tracker report. Only shops with the 'pay_whoever_asks' instruction pay.

eventCatalog.name: The neighbors upstairs call 311 about the music
eventCatalog.text: An inspector takes a decibel reading inside their apartment. Over 42 means a $2,000 ticket that you can cut to zero once by fixing the sound and filing a consultant's report.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 noise complaints against the address; open doors and windows in warm months
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Noise is the largest 311 complaint category in New York City; the share against cafes was not found
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic rule proposed: arrives in a warm month while the speaker shortcut is active, or with long hours and music on. That noise leads 311 categories is from memory of city data.

eventCatalog.name: Someone reports every sign on the avenue
eventCatalog.text: Dozens of 311 complaints about shop signs land in one week. Buildings inspectors work down the block; signs without permits get $6,000 fines.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 illegal-sign complaints by community district (NYC Open Data); the 2018-2019 surge led to Local Law 28 of 2019
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A citywide wave in 2018-2019, with fines of about $5,000-$6,000 per shop, prompted a temporary freeze and a task force
eventCatalog.note: Announced a month ahead to the whole block. The legal move is the setup item sign_permit_and_hanger or a sign of 6 square feet or less.

eventCatalog.name: Sanitation agents work your street
eventCatalog.text: Twice a day, in posted one-hour windows, agents can ticket a dirty sidewalk or gutter. Trash set out wrong and anything blocking the sidewalk can be ticketed at any hour.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DSNY enforcement routing times for the block (two one-hour periods a day for commercial premises)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every working day
eventCatalog.note: Not an event to announce: a standing fact of the street. Listed so the engine treats sanitation violations as found within the month they exist.

eventCatalog.name: The local fire company inspects the block
eventCatalog.text: Firefighters from the neighborhood firehouse walk through every shop: extinguisher tags, the exit path, extension cords, candles.
eventCatalog.realSignal: FDNY field inspection schedule for the administrative district
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found; FDNY says extinguishers are checked during every inspection for other permits
eventCatalog.note: Proposed as a yearly visit to every block, announced a month ahead. How often fire companies really reach a small cafe was not found.

eventCatalog.name: The yearly backflow test report is due
eventCatalog.text: Twelve months after the last report the city expects the next one. No report means a notice, then a $500 summons.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Date of the shop's last test report on file with Environmental Protection
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year for every property with a device; 8,780 violations for missing reports in 2018
eventCatalog.note: Falls in the anniversary month of opening. The $240 test price is my estimate; the pack's maintenance line already reserves for it, so the engine should not charge it twice.

eventCatalog.name: Yearly harassment training is due
eventCatalog.text: Every worker needs the interactive training once a year, and new hires as soon as possible. Free materials, one paid hour each.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Twelve months since the shop's last training round
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year for every employer in New York State
eventCatalog.note: One hour out of about 140 a month per worker is under 1% of hours; the multiplier is rounded.

eventCatalog.name: Health permit renewal
eventCatalog.text: The Food Service Establishment Permit expires a year after it was issued. Renewal costs $280, and unpaid city fines can hold it up.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Expiration date printed on the shop's permit
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year
eventCatalog.note: The $280 is verified in the pack; the pack's permit_renewals line already reserves for it, so the engine should not charge it twice. That unpaid fines can block a renewal is how owners describe it; I did not find the rule text.

eventCatalog.name: Lease anniversary: the rent steps up
eventCatalog.text: Most store leases raise the rent every year by a fixed percentage written into the lease. Month 13 costs more than month 12.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The escalation clause of the shop's own lease
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year of the lease
eventCatalog.note: Falls in the thirteenth month, so it matters for a second season or for a bought business. 3% a year is the figure brokers commonly quote for fixed steps; I did not verify it against a survey. The player's move is made at signing: a negotiated cap (roadmap step negotiate_lease_law_terms).

eventCatalog.name: The landlord bills your share of the property tax increase
eventCatalog.text: The city's assessment went up, and the lease passes a share of every increase over the base year to you as additional rent.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Department of Finance assessment roll and the tax rate set each June; bills run from July 1
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly wherever the lease has a tax escalation clause; reported leases set the tenant's share at 10% or 15% of the increase over a base year
eventCatalog.note: The 2% of rent is my estimate. The July date and the June rate-setting are from memory of the city's tax calendar. Unpaid additional rent is a lease default like unpaid rent.

eventCatalog.name: The lease ends: renew at the landlord's price or leave
eventCatalog.text: No law caps the new rent or gives you the right to stay. The build-out you paid for stays with the landlord.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Expiration date of the shop's lease; asking rents on the same street
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once per lease term of 5 to 10 years. In 2025 one Brooklyn cafe reported its rent nearly tripled and another an extra $4,000 a month; both closed
eventCatalog.note: Outside the first year unless the player buys a business with a short lease left. The engine clamps multipliers at 1.5; real resets range from none to nearly triple. A state bill to cap increases and guarantee 10-year renewals (S8319/A5568A) sat in committee in 2026.

eventCatalog.name: A 14-day rent demand is served
eventCatalog.text: You missed the rent. The landlord's process server delivers a written demand: pay within 14 days or give up the space. Next comes court, then a marshal.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own unpaid rent
eventCatalog.realFrequency: City marshals carried out about 10,900 commercial evictions from 2017 to 2025, 9% of all evictions (NYC Open Data dashboard)
eventCatalog.note: Follows from the player's own cash position, never from chance. Law seen: 14-day written demand (RPAPL §711(2)), then a nonpayment case, then a marshal's 14-day notice (RPAPL §749); paying everything owed before the eviction stops it. The four months from demand to lockout and the $1,500 of legal fees billed to the tenant under the lease are my estimates; no timeline statistic was found.

eventCatalog.name: The landlord wants the space back early
eventCatalog.text: Heat goes off, the hallway is 'under repair', your deliveries are blocked. It is cheaper for him than buying you out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A redevelopment plan or a richer tenant for the building
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A Manhattan community board wrote in 2025 that most harassed small-business owners cannot afford to sue; few cases reach court
eventCatalog.note: Commercial tenant harassment (Administrative Code §22-902) carries a civil penalty of $10,000 to $50,000 and lets the tenant sue; refusing to renew is not harassment. The 5% demand dip is my estimate. With the legal_help lever on, the pressure stops after one month.

eventCatalog.name: Staying past the end of the lease
eventCatalog.text: Talks dragged on and the lease ran out. Every extra month is billed at the holdover rate in the lease.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The holdover clause of the shop's own lease
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New York courts have enforced holdover clauses of 150% and 200% of the last rent
eventCatalog.note: The engine clamps multipliers at 1.5; leases reported in court decisions set 150%, 200%, or 150% rising to 200% after 30 days.
